name: Erik Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a chef for twenty years, the last eight as co-owner of a bistro by the harbour. Brilliant food, terrible hours, and I barely saw my kids awake. At 40 I sold my share to my business partner, which gave us a good cushion, and the electricity company down the coast was crying out for apprentices, so I went for it. I'm 43 now and in my third year. Claire, my wife, runs a hair salon in town, and we've got Léo, who's fifteen, and Anna, who's eleven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're a maintenance and storm crew on the coast, so the salt eats everything, and half our work is swapping corroded fittings and cross-arms before they fail. Then a big storm comes in off the sea and it's all hands, sixteen-hour shifts, lines down along the cliff road, and Sandra, our crew leader, running it like a busy Saturday service. I'm decent with the ropes now, still slow on the more technical connections, and Kofi, who's 29, has been very patient. I love the storm nights, oddly, it's the same rush as a full restaurant. What wears me out is the cold, and the feeling that at 43 I'm still the one being told how to hold the spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shrug and say, well, there you go, it was a fancy toaster after all. At work it'd be a two-minute joke over coffee in the van. I'm not someone who posts opinions online, I post pictures of what I cooked on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my move was the right one and I can stop wondering about it. Salt doesn't care about AI, and storms will keep knocking lines down. It's good news for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Finish my apprenticeship next year, maybe take the extra course in live-line work after that, because it pays better. Keep the bistro money where it is, a bit in savings, a bit in a fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a kitchen where the new oven turns out to be the same as the old one, you just keep cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Claire showed me how to ask it for meal plans for the week, which is funny for a chef, but it saves me thinking on a Sunday night. I've asked it about electrical stuff once or twice, but I'd never trust it over Sandra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that wishes it was bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for Claire's salon bookings, the paperwork drives her mad. But for my job, no, I don't need a robot. I need warmer gloves.

S0.say: He'd joke that AI was a fancy toaster after all and leave it at a two-minute laugh in the van. He doesn't post opinions online, only pictures of Sunday cooking.
S0.think: He thinks it proves his career move was right, since salt corrosion and storms don't care about AI. He can stop second-guessing the switch.
S0.do: Carries on and finishes his apprenticeship next year, then considers a better-paid live-line course. Keeps the bistro money split between savings and a fund.
S0.feel: Calm, like a kitchen where the new oven turns out the same as the old one.
S0.quote: I don't need a robot. I need warmer gloves.
S0.fieldNote: Erik's voice is practical and full of kitchen comparisons. He uses AI lightly for meal plans and trusts people over it. The plateau confirms his move and changes nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new kit: some of it's good, some of it's rubbish, and you work out which is which. At work I'd say we'll probably get drones checking the lines and maybe some clever scheduling, and that's fine. I'd tell my friends from the restaurant days to watch out, though, because ordering and stock are the kind of thing that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we're fine, mostly. Somebody still has to go up the pole on the cliff road at two in the morning in a gale. The bit I'd watch is whether the company uses it to run fewer crews and longer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others on the crew were using whatever the company brought in, I'd learn it too, properly. I'd finish my ticket, and then do the live-line course, because that's more skilled and harder to replace. We'd keep saving as normal, nothing drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with one eye open. It feels like change I've seen before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it once the others were using it. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been the first to buy fancy kit before. I bought a sous-vide machine for the bistro in the early days, very expensive, and it sat in the corner for a year because nobody had time to learn it. Now I wait until someone shows me it really works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Claire's salon in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People still want a person cutting their hair, so I think the salon's all right. The bookings and stock will probably go on some AI system, and honestly she'd love that. She hates the admin.

S1.say: He'd say new AI is like any new kit, some good and some rubbish, and expect drones and smarter scheduling. He'd warn restaurant friends that ordering and stock jobs go first.
S1.think: He thinks lineworkers are mostly fine because someone still climbs on the cliff road in a gale at night. He'd watch for the company running fewer crews on longer shifts.
S1.do: Learns the company's new tools properly once the rest of the crew uses them. Finishes his ticket, then takes the live-line course to become harder to replace, and keeps saving as normal.
S1.quote: I bought a sous-vide machine for the bistro in the early days, very expensive, and it sat in the corner for a year because nobody had time to learn it.
S1.fieldNote: Erik's caution about new tech comes from a concrete, slightly comic restaurant story. He sees the salon and his own job as safe because people want people. His one worry is crew size and shift length.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and nobody knows how it'll play out, so let's not pretend we do. I'd tell people to keep their heads and look after their families. I wouldn't be one for marching, but I'd want the government to come up with something quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. I'm a third-year apprentice who'd barely be qualified, and the salon's customers might not have jobs either, so Claire's income gets hit too. We have the bistro money, so we wouldn't go under quickly, but a cushion is for a fall, not for a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Claire and work out how many months we can last if both incomes drop by half. I'd stop paying extra into the fund and keep that money as cash. I'd keep going to work, and I'd look at whether I could do private dinners or cooking for events on weekends, because people might still want a real cook at a wedding even if a robot can make dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years of warning change it, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is like getting a booking for two hundred people with an hour's notice. You don't plan, you just react and hope the fridge is full. Luckily our fridge is fairly full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lie awake doing sums. Which sum keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Léo's university. He wants to study engineering in three years, and I'd be lying there wondering whether that's still a job by the time he finishes, and whether we should spend that money on it at all. That's the one I couldn't answer.

S2.say: He'd say it's a huge shock and nobody really knows how it plays out, so people should keep their heads and look after their families. He wouldn't march but would want quick government action.
S2.think: He'd be worried as a barely qualified apprentice, with Claire's salon customers also losing jobs. The bistro money would keep them afloat for a while, but it's a cushion, not a life.
S2.do: Works out with Claire how long they can last if both incomes halve, and moves fund contributions into cash. Keeps working and looks into weekend private dinners and event cooking as a side income.
S2.feel: Anxious and lying awake doing sums, but not falling apart.
S2.quote: A cushion is for a fall, not for a life.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's strong cushion keeps him steady, but he's clear it only buys time. His fallback is his old trade, and he thinks people may still pay for a real cook at a wedding. Léo's university plans are the sum he can't solve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're sensible, and people should start now. At work I'd suggest we ask the company straight out what it's planning. I'd say the government should be setting up some kind of support for people who lose their jobs, but I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I qualify and get a few years of good money first. That matters, because we can put most of it away. I'd be 48 when it lands, which is young enough to try something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify next year and do the live-line course, because better pay means more to save. I'd start the private dinners on the side in year two or three, small, maybe once a month, to see if people would pay. And once I'd seen what the AI tools actually do well, I'd use them to plan menus and bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with my sleeves rolled up. Five years is a proper prep list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a cooking business really survive if AI and robots can do almost anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe rich people would pay more for a human chef, the way they pay more for handmade furniture. Or maybe not, and it's just a hobby that pays for itself, which would still be something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, funnily enough, even though he's young and great at the job. He's put everything into this trade, he's got a baby on the way, and he's never done anything else. I've got a second string to my bow, he hasn't.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, suggest asking the company straight out about its plans, and want government support set up, without shouting about it.
S3.think: He thinks five years gives him a qualification and a few years of good money to put away, and at 48 he'd still be young enough to try something else.
S3.do: Qualifies next year and takes the live-line course for better pay to save. Starts small monthly private dinners in year two or three, and uses AI tools for menus and bookings once he's seen what they do well.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but ready to work through it like a prep list.
S3.quote: Maybe rich people would pay more for a human chef, the way they pay more for handmade furniture.
S3.fieldNote: Erik is honest that his side business may not survive AGI and is fine with it being a hobby that pays for itself. He worries more for a younger colleague with no second skill. Five years turns him from reacting to prepping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if we use it, and I'd hope the government does. At work I'd say it's far enough off that we should just keep doing good work. With friends I'd say the same, plan a bit, don't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels all right. I'd have most of a decade as a lineworker, the kids would be grown, and I'd be 53 with savings. That's not a bad place to face a big change from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, do live-line work, and save hard. I'd build the cooking on the side slowly, maybe a proper small catering business by year five or six. And we'd sit down with Léo and Anna about what they study, trying to pick things that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry for the kids, not much for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you suggest the kids study, if you had to guess today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something with people and hands together. Léo wants engineering, and I'd say fine, but make it the kind where you're on site, not just at a screen. Anna's into animals, and I'd tell her a vet still needs to hold the dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what does the extra time change most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes me from a cook in the weeds to a cook with a prep list. That's kitchen talk for drowning in orders versus being ready. In two years I'm just grabbing things. In ten, I can actually decide what I want to be doing at 53.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time if it's used well and hope the government does. At work he'd say keep doing good work, and with friends he'd say plan a bit and don't lose sleep.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is all right: most of a decade as a lineworker, grown kids, and savings by 53. That's a decent place to face a big change from.
S4.do: Qualifies, does live-line work and saves hard while slowly building a small catering business by year five or six. Talks with Léo and Anna about studying things that need a person.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry for the kids and little for himself.
S4.quote: It changes me from a cook in the weeds to a cook with a prep list.
S4.fieldNote: Erik is pragmatic and steady, and the extra years let him plan his own path. His side business grows naturally out of his past. His advice to the kids leans towards work that combines people and hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years means no time to qualify, no time to build anything on the side, and both Claire's salon and my job hit at once. What would help is clear information early, from the company and the government, about what's coming and when, and some support for people while they switch, so a cushion like ours doesn't have to be a whole life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about what people would do with their time. If nobody needs us to work, someone has to cook dinner for the family and the neighbours, and I'd quite like that to still be me. Work isn't just money, it's what you're useful for.

headlineQuote: Work isn't just money, it's what you're useful for.
portrait: Erik Moreau is a 43-year-old third-year apprentice on a coastal maintenance and storm crew, after twenty years as a chef and co-owner of a harbour bistro. Selling his share gave the family a solid cushion, and his wife Claire runs a hair salon. He's pragmatic, waits until new tools are proven, and explains everything through kitchen comparisons. Calm in the plateau and steady change, he becomes anxious when AGI arrives in two years because both household incomes would be hit at once. With five or ten years he saves hard, takes the live-line course and slowly builds a cooking business on the side, while worrying most about his son's university plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to qualify or build anything on the side, and both his job and Claire's salon would be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, early information from the company and government about what's coming and when, and support for people while they switch.
